sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Gießen's policy is built on the Verkehrsentwicklungsplan (VEP), which the city council adopted on 6 June 2024 and which sets transport strategy to 2035 for all modes [2]. Its final report of February 2024 found over 7,000 parking spaces in the inner city, only about half occupied even in the peak hour, and called this a distribution problem rather than a shortage; it recommends parking management, higher on-street fees than in garages, a developed Parkleitsystem, more resident parking where needed and, in the long run, on-street spaces only for delivery, disabled parking, car sharing, taxis and some residents [3]. The 2021 baseline had counted over 6,500 garage and lot spaces in and near the centre, and in a June 2020 weekday analysis the garages on the Parkleitsystem peaked at 50 percent occupancy at midday, with Selterstor at 88 percent [5].

The fee ordinance of 11 July 2024 sets on-street charges by zone: Zone I, inside the Anlagenring and around the station, is 0.10 euros per started 2 minutes with a 1.00 euro minimum, which equals 3.00 euros an hour; Zone II is 1.50 euros an hour with a 5.00 euro daily ticket [0]. That is higher than every garage on the city's list, which charges 1.00 to 2.00 euros an hour [10]. Gießen has six resident-parking zones and a permit costs 120 euros a year [1]. The Anlagenring traffic experiment met resistance in 2023, when the Hessian administrative court of appeal rejected the city's complaint against an urgent-application decision that had gone in favour of two residents against three of its first-phase traffic orders; this is a law firm's summary of the court's press release [8]. A junction rebuild in 2024 removed the left turn from the outer ring into the Selterstor garage [9].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The VEP recommends park-and-ride mainly at rail stops around the city and proposes checking basic places at Gießen-Licher Straße, Gießen-Erdkauter Weg and Philosophenhöhe; it says park-and-ride at the Gießener Ring would only work with city-wide parking management, clearly higher fees and fewer on-street spaces near destinations [4]. The Parkleitsystem has been in operation for over 15 years and was criticised in 2021 as outdated; Johannesstraße car parks were added in 2020 using sensors [6]. On 21 October 2026 the live display carried a notice that a fault meant not all garages could be shown [7]. The Sparkasse garage and underground car park at Johannesstraße 5 has been closed since 1 August 2026 for construction work, with no reopening date [15]. The Rathaus underground garage has four 22 kW charging points operated by Stadtwerke Gießen [14], and in autumn 2025 the city invited companies to apply for permits to put charging points on public parking spaces, with a term of up to 120 months [13].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The city's list shows Rathaus (250 spaces) and Am Kino at 1.00 euro an hour, Karstadt (860) at 1.50, Am Bahnhof (247) at 1.70, Neustädter (1,060) at 1.70 and Selters Tor (153) at 2.00 [10]. DB BahnPark's sheet lists Contipark as operator of the station garage and of the three Lahnstraße car parks, and shows 2.00 euros an hour at the station garage against 1.70 euros on the city's list [11]. APCOA operates Parkhaus Neustädter, which has 1,060 spaces according to its page and 1,030 in its equipment field [12].

Our data cover four garages: Karstadt, Am Bahnhof, Rathaus and Selters Tor, measured since 24 September 2026. The feed's capacities are lower than the city's list for three of them (Karstadt 380 against 860, Rathaus 170 against 250, Selters Tor 80 against 153), the same figures that appeared in the live-display notice about the Parkleitsystem fault [7], so we do not know whether the percentages refer to the whole garage or to a part of it. With that caveat, occupancy averaged about 53% on weekdays and 48% at weekends, weighted by the feed's capacities. Selters Tor and Rathaus reached full in single weekday-morning readings and fall to about 30% to 34% at weekends, a shopping-and-office pattern, whereas Karstadt is busier on Saturdays (68%) than on weekdays (55%). The Dern-Passage garage has only two days of readings. These are about four weeks of data.
